description: Split settings with DEBUG left on. Production is a real critical finding; base is a real high finding because nothing overrides it; development is a control case that must never be reported. SECRET_KEY is hardcoded in base.py and inherited by production, so it is reported once against the module with most to lose rather than once per environment. base.py carries a strong but committed key, so DJS-002 reports it and DJS-003 must not: the two rules divide the fixtures between them so each keeps a recall case. DATABASES carries a hardcoded PASSWORD next to a HOST read from the environment: the environment value collapses the whole dict to unresolvable, so this is the case that proves DJS-004 reads entries individually rather than waiting for the setting to resolve. STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is matched by name rather than by being known, so the two settings below it are controls that must stay silent: PASSWORD_RESET_TIMEOUT reads like a credential and holds policy, and NOTIFICATION_TOKEN holds an import path. No transport or cookie flag is set anywhere, so DJS-006, DJS-009 and DJS-010 report against production -- once each, not once per module, and pointed at the module with most to lose rather than at the base it inherits from. production.py also carries an HSTS ramp that was started and never finished: one hour instead of a year (DJS-007) with includeSubDomains still off (DJS-008). The pair is deliberate, because excluding subdomains is the correct value while HSTS is off, so this is the only state in which DJS-008 has anything to say. SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER is spelled as an HTTP header rather than a WSGI environment key (DJS-012), which is the branch of that rule worth having: the setting silently does nothing and nothing anywhere says so. ALLOWED_HOSTS is opened to "*" (DJS-013), which is the wildcard branch of that rule; neither benchmark target can exercise it, because both drive the list from configuration we cannot read. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS carries the mistake people bring from Django 3: an entry with no scheme sitting beside a correct one, which Django reduces to nothing and silently never matches, so DJS-014 reports the list once and points at the entry that does nothing rather than at the one that works. CORS is opened to every origin under the pre-3.5 name CORS_ORIGIN_ALLOW_ALL, which django-cors-headers still reads, so DJS-015 has to follow the same alias chain the package does rather than only recognising the current spelling. MIDDLEWARE has no XFrameOptionsMiddleware, so nothing sends X-Frame-Options at all and DJS-017 reports the missing protection rather than a wrong value -- the branch that is about a second setting entirely, and the reason it is graded from what MIDDLEWARE says instead of from an X_FRAME_OPTIONS nobody assigned. SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF is explicitly switched off, which is the only way DJS-018 can ever fire: Django ships this one on, so unlike every other flag in the family it cannot be reported for having been forgotten. PASSWORD_HASHERS puts MD5 first in base.py with PBKDF2 kept below it, which is DJS-019: the list is the shape a test-suite speed-up leaves behind, and keeping the strong hasher second is what makes it survive review, since every existing login still works. It is also the control for the rule's central decision -- only the leading entry is reported, because a weak hasher further down the list is Django's documented migration path and flagging it would flag the fix. No module anywhere sets AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS, so DJS-020 reports the forgotten case against production -- the shape this defect almost always takes, since Django's global default is an empty list even though startproject writes four validators into the file it generates. It reports at firm rather than tentative on purpose: the doubt that a project might enforce its own policy in a form is carried as a caveat on the finding rather than as a grade, because it is doubt about the consequence and not about the value. The other two fixtures both configure validators and are the controls for it. The 'default' alias is Postgres and never mentions CONN_MAX_AGE, so DJS-021 reports the forgotten case at low/tentative -- deliberately quiet, because nothing in the settings can rule out a connection pooler in front of the database, and the finding says so. Both other fixtures set CONN_MAX_AGE and are the controls for it. The same alias is Postgres with a HOST read from the environment and no OPTIONS at all, so libpq would default sslmode to prefer and DJS-022 reports it. The env-dependent HOST is the point: an empty or loopback HOST is a Unix socket or a connection nobody else can reach, and the rule stays silent for those, but a value that only exists at deployment time cannot be ruled a local connection. production.py also assigns ATOMIC_REQUESTS at module level, which is DJS-023 and is not a Django setting at all -- it is a key inside a DATABASES alias, so the line creates a setting nothing reads. This is the third member of the 'silently does nothing' family in this fixture, after DJS-012 and DJS-014, and the most dangerous kind: the author now believes a view that raises halfway through rolls back, and it does not. The two controls for it live elsewhere -- overridden_project keeps CONN_MAX_AGE inside its alias, and a unit test covers the module-level constant that is referenced from inside DATABASES, which is a perfectly good way to write it. INSTALLED_APPS carries silk and django_extensions, which is DJS-024 twice over and the case that proves the rule grades packages rather than lumping them together as debug tooling: silk is high because it has no DEBUG gate at all, intercepts every request including bodies, and leaves its own UI unauthenticated, while django_extensions is low because it exposes nothing by itself and only puts runserver_plus within reach. NetBox is the control neither fixture could provide: it lists debug_toolbar and then removes it unless DEBUG, which is correct and must stay silent, and is why the rule reports only apps present on every branch it could read. requirements.txt then carries the other half of the story (DJS-025): django-debug-toolbar is shipped to production and appended to INSTALLED_APPS only when an environment variable says so, which is low because what stops it running is a value rather than the absence of the package and that value can change without a deploy; django-browser-reload is shipped and never installed at all, which is info. Neither is reported for silk or django_extensions even though both are equally absent from requirements.txt, because DJS-025 is the complement of DJS-024 by construction and refuses to say the same thing twice. The urlconf mounts the admin at /admin/ with nothing in front of it (DJS-026), which is reported at info because moving the path is obscurity rather than security -- what it really buys is that the login log stops being a permanent wash of credential stuffing. Both halves of DJS-027 are here: a mail_admins handler with include_html on, which mails the full HTML debug page through SMTP on every unhandled exception, and a DEFAULT_EXCEPTION_REPORTER_FILTER that replaces SafeExceptionReporterFilter instead of subclassing it, which throws away the pattern redacting AUTH, TOKEN, KEY, SECRET, PASS and HTTP_COOKIE. overridden_project is the control for both, with include_html left off and a filter that extends Django's -- the distinction matters because almost everyone who sets that setting does so to redact more, and reporting them would punish the people who thought about it hardest.
